props.title: Totally F***ed Up
props.initialSlug: Gay teens navigate life & love in LA underground

sections.content: Gregg Araki's **Totally F***ed Up** (1993) marks a pivotal moment in New Queer Cinema, following six LGBTQ+ teenagers in Los Angeles with raw authenticity. Shot in a pseudo-documentary style that predates similar techniques in **Kids** (1995), Araki captures teenage alienation through a distinctly queer lens. The film forms part of Araki's "Teenage Apocalypse Trilogy," alongside **The Doom Generation** (1995) and **Nowhere** (1997), establishing his signature mix of nihilistic youth culture, punk aesthetics, and bold sexuality.

sections.content: The film's experimental structure, divided into 15 segments, influenced later LGBTQ+ cinema like **Weekend** (2011) and **Moonlight** (2016). Araki's use of handheld cameras and direct-to-camera confessionals creates an intimacy that feels remarkably current, predating the social media era's obsession with personal documentation. The raw emotional honesty of **Totally F***ed Up** laid groundwork for films like **But I'm a Cheerleader** (1999) and **The Perks of Being a Wallflower** (2012).

The film's exploration of Gen X disaffection parallels contemporaneous works like **Slacker** (1990) and **Reality Bites** (1994), but through a distinctly queer perspective. Araki's characters grapple with suicide, homophobia, and AIDS while maintaining a dark humor that would influence later filmmakers like Xavier Dolan in **I Killed My Mother** (2009) and **Heartbeats** (2010). sections.content: Araki's guerrilla filmmaking style and modest budget of $100,000 helped establish a template for independent queer cinema. The film's influence can be seen in works like **Shortbus** (2006) and **Keep the Lights On** (2012), which maintain similar raw approaches to sexuality and emotional authenticity. The mixing of formats and experimental narrative structure also influenced later digital-age storytelling in films like **Tangerine** (2015).
